title: Compression, CDN & Connection Reuse in Practice
objectives: Choose between gzip and Brotli based on ratio, CPU cost and caching
Design a Cache-Control strategy for HTML, hashed assets and APIs
Explain how CDN edge caching and keep-alive cut latency
Measure TTFB and transferred bytes before and after each change
body:
Once the connection exists, two levers decide how fast bytes arrive: how many bytes you send (compression) and where they come from (cache proximity). Neither is a single setting — they are policies you apply per resource type, and every policy has a failure mode you must design against.

## The problem
Your app serves 900 KB of JavaScript and a 40 KB HTML document from a single origin far from most users. First loads are slow and repeat visits are barely faster, because nothing is cached well and compression was enabled with defaults nobody reviewed.

## Constraints
- Brotli compresses text 15–20% smaller than gzip, but its highest quality levels are too slow for on-the-fly compression.
- Images, videos and woff2 fonts are already compressed; recompressing wastes CPU and can even grow them.
- A long `max-age` on unversioned files serves stale content until the cache expires — correctness first, then speed.
- CDN hit ratio depends on your URLs: a query string that varies per user fragments the cache.

## Options
A per-resource-type strategy, stated as a table:

| Resource | Cache-Control | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTML (entry) | `no-cache` (revalidate) | Always fresh routes, still fast with ETags |
| Hashed JS/CSS | `max-age=31536000, immutable` | Filename changes when content changes |
| Fonts/images | `max-age=31536000` | Content-addressed URLs |
| User API JSON | `no-store` or short `private, max-age=0` | Personalized, must not be shared-cached |

Compression pairing: Brotli quality 4–5 for dynamic responses, quality 10–11 for files compressed once at build time, gzip as the fallback for old clients.

## Tradeoffs
Immutable caching is only safe when the build pipeline really changes URLs on content change — otherwise users are stuck with stale assets until the TTL lapses. On-the-fly Brotli at quality 11 can cost more CPU than it saves, so it belongs in the build, not the request path. CDNs add a cache invalidation surface: wrong `Vary` or `Cache-Control` headers are amplified to every edge node.

## Decision
Compress all text (HTML, JS, CSS, SVG, JSON) with Brotli, precompressed at build time where possible. Version hashed assets and mark them immutable; keep HTML revalidating. Put a CDN in front and keep user-specific data off shared cache keys. Reuse connections — keep-alive is the default you should never opt out of.

## Measure it
TTFB is the before/after metric for edge and caching work; transferred bytes (not original size) is the metric for compression. Check the `content-encoding` and `age` response headers, CDN cache-status headers, and record the Network panel waterfall for the same URL from the same location before and after.

## Best practices
- Precompress static assets with Brotli at build time; compress dynamic text at quality 4–5.
- Never compress already-compressed formats; the CPU cost buys nothing.
- Use `immutable` only with content-hashed filenames.
- Mark personalized responses `private` so CDNs never share them.
- Keep-alive on, HTTP/2 on, and measure TTFB per resource class before and after.

## Common mistakes
- Setting `max-age=31536000` on HTML and wondering why deploys do not reach users.
- Serving the same `Cache-Control` for every path instead of per resource class.
- Enabling gzip but forgetting SVG and JSON, then measuring only the JS bundle.
- Cache-busting with random query strings, which defeats CDN caching instead of using versions.
- Declaring the CDN faster without comparing TTFB from the same client location before and after.

examples.name: cache-headers.sh
examples.code:
# Inspect what the server actually sends: encoding, caching, CDN hits.
curl -sI https://app.example.com/assets/app.a83f2c.js | findstr /i "content-encoding cache-control age cf-cache-status"
# content-encoding: br          <- Brotli in use
cache-control: max-age=31536000, immutable
# age: 84531                    <- served from edge cache

# Compare sizes: original vs gzip vs brotli for one asset.
curl -s https://app.example.com/assets/app.a83f2c.js -o app.js
# then compress locally with your build tool and compare byte counts:
#   app.js           912 KB   (identity)
#   app.js.gz        268 KB   (gzip -9)
#   app.js.br        221 KB   (brotli -q 11)

# HTML must revalidate: it references the hashed assets.
curl -sI https://app.example.com/ | findstr /i "cache-control etag"
# cache-control: no-cache
# etag: "7f4a2e"               <- revalidation is a cheap 304 when unchanged

exercise.prompt: Build a cacheability and transfer-size analyzer. For each asset (with original size, encoding and Cache-Control), render: the estimated transferred size (identity = 100%, gzip = 35%, br = 30% of original) and a cache verdict — revalidate (no-cache), hard-cache (max-age of a year with immutable), short-cache (any other max-age), or never-store (no-store). The size estimate and verdict functions are stubbed.
hints: Pick the ratio with a small lookup object keyed by encoding, defaulting to 1.
no-cache and no-store are different verdicts: revalidate vs never-store.
Hard-cache means the header contains immutable; a plain max-age is only short-cache.

questions.prompt: Why should you not gzip or Brotli-compress an already-compressed woff2 font?
options: Browsers reject Content-Encoding on font files
It wastes CPU for no size win and can slightly increase the size
It breaks the font file checksum
Compression is only allowed for HTML and CSS
questions.explanation: woff2, images and video are already entropy-coded; recompressing them burns server CPU while producing little or no reduction.

questions.prompt: Which response is the correct pair for hashed static assets versus the HTML entry document?
questions.explanation: Hashed filenames change when content changes, so they can be cached hard; the HTML must revalidate because it is the document that points at the current asset versions.
